builder_plan.scenario: A self-hosted assistant is too expensive because its model uses most of the GPU memory.
builder_plan.change: Try the paper's supported lower-precision weights on a copy of your serving setup.
builder_plan.baseline: The same model at its original precision, on the same GPU.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Peak memory, task pass rate, latency, and total serving cost at the same context and load.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: SHq: Learnable Grids for LLM Weight Quantization
summary: SHq replaces the fixed lookup-table grids (INT, FP, NF, BOF) in block-scaled LUT quantization formats such as NF4, BOF4, and NVFP4 with a closed-form grid parameterized by a companding strength and an offset, requiring only modification of table contents. It costs a per-format grid selection or fitting step and reuses the otherwise-unused sign bit of the FP8 block scale; it adds no runtime latency or memory overhead since it is a drop-in grid replacement. It can fail if downstream kernels or hardware LUT instructions hardcode specific grids, if the optimal parameters do not transfer across models or layers, or if gains measured in KL divergence do not hold for the reader's specific tasks at very low bit-widths.
rationale: It is a zero-overhead drop-in improvement for LUT quantization the reader may already use, but gains should be validated on their own models and serving stack before adoption.
technique: Learnable LUT grids for block-scaled weight quantization

claims.statement: SHq replaces the fixed lookup-table grids (INT, FP, NF, BOF) in block-scaled LUT quantization formats such as NF4, BOF4, and NVFP4 with a closed-form grid parameterized by a companding strength and an offset, requiring only modification of table contents. It costs a per-format grid selection or fitting step and reuses the otherwise-unused sign bit of the FP8 block scale; it adds no runtime latency or memory overhead since it is a drop-in grid replacement. It can fail if downstream kernels or hardware LUT instructions hardcode specific grids, if the optimal parameters do not transfer across models or layers, or if gains measured in KL divergence do not hold for the reader's specific tasks at very low bit-widths.

SHq achieves the lowest KL divergence at 3 and 4 bits across five models (3B-35B), outperforming the best fixed grid by up to 34% and reducing NVFP4 KL divergence by 41-67% at 4.5 bits per weight while improving downstream accuracy.
